WorkspaceInvitationsRecord.description:
A pending invitation, one row per workspace and email_key (unique index), whether or not an account exists yet for that address. Fields: workspace (relation, required, removed with its workspace), email (the address as typed, trimmed and lowercased), email_key (hidden, and the ONLY column ever compared: trimmed, lowercased, and for gmail.com and googlemail.com only with every dot in the local part and everything from the first plus sign to the at sign dropped, the same fold users.email_key uses, so an invitation means the same address as an account), role (admin, member or viewer) and invited_by (relation to users, optional, no cascade, so an admin leaving the workspace does not revoke a grant the workspace made). See decision:invitation-keyed-by-email.

**Access.** create is the workspace owner, or an ACTIVE admin who may invite only as member. list, view and delete are the workspace owner and its ACTIVE admins only, narrower than the membership roster, because a pending invitation is an administrative act in progress. update is null: an invitation is revoked and re-issued, never edited. Every rule carries a workspace-not-trashed conjunct, so a trashed workspace resolves nobody. A request that names a workspace (?workspace=) can view or delete an invitation only if it belongs to that workspace; otherwise it answers 404.

**Limits.** Sends are capped per inviter per rolling day and a decline blocks a repeat invitation from that workspace for a while; see collection:invitation_events and decision:invitation-send-limit-and-decline-block.

**Expiry.** One app_settings row, invitation_expiry_days (default 7), sizes the window. A daily cron sweep deletes rows past it, and the accept route re-checks it itself, so an already-expired invitation cannot be accepted between sweeps. Every list and view also returns expires_at (created plus invitation_expiry_days in whole days, 7 when that setting is missing, non-numeric or negative) and expired (true once now reaches expires_at); both are computed on read and not stored.

**Accept and decline.** POST /api/tracker/invitations/{id}/accept is open to the invitee only, matched on the folded email_key of the caller. It creates the workspace_members row at status active in the same transaction that deletes the invitation; when the caller already holds a membership there, that row is left exactly as it is, so a suspended member is never reactivated by accepting. POST /api/tracker/invitations/{id}/decline deletes the invitation and creates nothing. Both refuse an unknown id, an invitation addressed to someone else, or a trashed workspace with the identical 404 an unknown id gets, so neither route is an existence oracle.

**Mine.** GET /api/tracker/invitations/mine answers which invitations belong to the caller. It is a route rather than a collection rule because email_key is hidden on users and PocketBase drops hidden fields from filter matching, so a rule attempting that comparison would return an empty 200 for everyone.

email_key.description: Hidden system field — not returned in API responses.

WorkspaceMembersRecord.description:
Links a user to a workspace, one row per workspace and user (unique index). Fields: workspace (relation, required, removed with its workspace), user (relation, required, removed with the user), role (select, required: admin, member or viewer) and status (select, required: active or suspended). An update that sends an empty or invalid role is refused with HTTP 400 and a field-level validation_required error, so every row carries exactly one role.

**Only an active membership carries access.** Every membership branch of every workspace-scoped rule, list and view included, carries a same-row active-status conjunct beside its user check, so a suspended member gets a filtered-empty list, 404 on view, update and delete, and 400 on create, everywhere. Branches that grant on another basis stay ungated: workspace and record ownership, and the author and self paths. No branch grants on assignment, so a suspended member who is still the assignee of a task keeps no access to it. See decision:active-membership-grants-access.

**Viewer writes only on an assigned task.** A viewer keeps every read a member has, and the membership branch that grants each create, update and delete across tasks, milestones, decisions, documents, comments, projects, saved_views and task_subscribers carries a role-is-not-viewer guard on the same membership row as the user check, so a member and an admin pass and a viewer is excluded. A task assigned to a viewer grants them no write: they may not edit it, comment on it, react to its comments, subscribe to it or add subtasks under it. Admin-only branches are untouched.

**How a row is created.** The createRule is null, so no caller creates a membership through the collections API. A row comes into existence when the invited person accepts a pending invitation (POST /api/tracker/invitations/{id}/accept, see collection:workspace_invitations), which writes status active; when the caller already holds a membership in that workspace, accepting leaves that row untouched, so a suspended member is never reactivated by accepting. Every workspace create, through the collections API or a provisioning path, also gives the workspace owner a self-membership with role admin and status active. A membership created without a role is a member.

**Read.** The roster is open to the workspace OWNER and any ACTIVE member, and any user may read their own membership row whatever its status.

**Update.** The workspace owner may change role and status; an ACTIVE admin may change status but not role. Neither workspace nor user may change. Status moves only from active to suspended and from suspended back to active, superusers included; any other value or move is refused with HTTP 400 and a plain message (pb_hooks/membership_status.pb.js).

**The owner row is fixed.** Neither the owner nor an admin may change the role, status, workspace or user of the membership row that belongs to the workspace owner, or delete it: each answers HTTP 409 with a field-level last_active_owner error. A change that leaves the row admin and active is allowed, so an owner whose row was member when ownership arrived can raise it. A superuser is exempt, so an operator can still repair a roster. Ownership moves only through POST /api/tracker/workspaces/{id}/transfer-ownership (see route:workspaces-transfer-ownership), after which the row of the new owner is fixed and the row of the previous owner can be changed like any other.

**Delete.** The workspace owner or an ACTIVE admin removes a member, and any member or admin may leave by deleting their own row; leaving is not an escalation, so a SUSPENDED member may still leave. The workspace OWNER cannot leave: transfer ownership or delete the workspace first. A member who leaves or is removed has their assigned tasks unassigned (see decision:leaver-tasks-unassigned).

**Workspace scope.** A request that names a workspace (?workspace=) can view, update or delete a membership only if it belongs to that workspace; otherwise it answers 404. A request that names no workspace follows the usual rules.

**Workspace trash.** While the workspace holding them is in the trash, membership rows are frozen: an update or a delete, leaving included, answers exactly as an unknown id does for every caller, so a member can leave again once the workspace is restored. Reading them narrows to the set that can restore the workspace, its owner and an active admin, with no carve-out for a user reading their own row; every other tier gets an empty listing and the unknown-id answer. Nothing is written on the rows, so restoring the workspace brings them back unchanged.

WorkspacesRecord.description:
The tenancy layer: user, then workspace, then project, then item. Fields: name (required), owner (relation to users, required, removed with the user), priorities (json: the pickable priority vocabulary), default_project (relation to projects, optional) and trashed (date). A workspace is addressed only by its opaque record id, so name is display-only: renaming moves no address and two workspaces may share a name. A name made only of whitespace is refused with a 400 error by pb_hooks/names.pb.js.

**Access.** list and view are open to the OWNER and its ACTIVE members; a suspended member cannot list or view the workspace at all. create is any authenticated user: owner may be omitted and the server stamps the signed-in caller; a submitted owner must be the caller, and naming anyone else is refused with a 400 error; a superuser keeps the owner it submits. update is the owner or an ACTIVE admin, and an update that sends owner is refused, so ownership moves only through POST /api/tracker/workspaces/{id}/transfer-ownership. delete is owner-only. Deleting your last workspace provisions a fresh one with its seeded statuses, labels and priorities.

**Landing and switching.** GET /api/tracker/me/landing names the workspace a signed-in user should open, as {landing: {workspace, reason, invitation}} or {landing: null} when there is nowhere to go. It takes, in order: the earliest-created workspace the user owns that is not trashed (reason owned); else the workspace of their earliest active membership that is not trashed (member); else the workspace of their earliest invitation that has not expired, in a workspace that is not trashed and where they hold no membership (invitation, and invitation carries that invitation id, because the user cannot open the workspace until they accept); else the workspace of their earliest membership that is not trashed, which by then is a suspended one (suspended). GET /api/tracker/workspaces/{id}/switch answers whether the caller may open that workspace, as {workspace, allowed, reason, invitation}: allowed for its owner and its active members; otherwise reason is suspended for a suspended member and not_found for everyone else, the same answer for a workspace that does not exist, one the caller cannot read and one in the trash, so the route reveals nothing a workspace read would not. When the answer is not_found and the caller holds an invitation to that workspace, expired or not, invitation is {id, expired}, so a client shows the invitation to accept or decline instead of sending the user to their landing; otherwise it is null. Both routes answer a signed-in user, a request without one with 401, and a superuser with 403. See decision:landing-and-switch-check.

**Provisioning.** Every workspace, however it is created, gets its shadow project (concept:shadow-project), five default statuses, three core labels and, when priorities is empty or missing, the default priorities urgent, high, medium and low, from one after-create seeder in pb_hooks/main.pb.js. See decision:default-priority-vocabulary.

**Priority vocabulary.** priorities is a JSON array of entries shaped {id, name}, most severe first. A task stores the id of its entry (an empty string for no priority), never the name, so renaming or reordering an entry changes no task, and a name may carry any character, a comma included. An entry sent without an id keeps the id of the stored entry with the same name unless that id is sent on another entry, and otherwise gets a fresh server-minted 15-character id of lowercase letters and digits; a supplied id must have that shape and may not repeat. Every name is trimmed before it is checked and stored. Every HTTP write is validated entry by entry and answers 400 on a non-array value, an entry that is not an object, a blank or non-string name, a malformed or repeated id, a name repeated exactly, or any casing of the reserved token none. A CASE VARIANT of another entry is ACCEPTED: High alongside high is two entries, matching the binary-collated unique indexes of statuses and labels. An UPDATE may not empty the vocabulary or send null, because nothing re-seeds on update; a CREATE may, because the seeder replaces it with the defaults. Programmatic writers write repo-controlled literals and are not re-validated. A task write whose priority is not the id of a current entry, a name included, is refused 400 with code priority_not_in_vocabulary, while a task holding the id of a removed entry keeps it and stays writable on its other fields. No priority is the UNSET state, not an entry, and is always accepted.

**Trash.** The first DELETE moves a workspace to the trash; a second DELETE on a trashed workspace purges it. A PATCH that sets or re-dates trashed is refused with 400, so only the owner, with a DELETE, moves a workspace into the trash; a superuser is exempt. GET /api/tracker/workspaces/{id}/deletion-impact tells the owner beforehand what the workspace holds (route:workspaces-deletion-impact). A trashed workspace drops out of list and view for every caller; the owner and its active admins find it through GET /api/tracker/workspaces/trash and restore it with a PATCH clearing trashed. A daily cron purges workspaces trashed longer than app_settings.trash_retention_days.

While a workspace is in the trash, the work inside it, its projects and their tasks, documents, decisions and milestones, with the edit history and subscriptions that hang off them, is hidden from every member, the owner and an active admin included, and frozen so none of it can be created, edited or deleted. Unsubscribing from a task stays available throughout. Its configuration is frozen too: statuses, labels, cycles, templates, saved views and the member list refuse every create, update and delete, and reading them narrows to the owner and an ACTIVE admin. Nothing inside is stamped, so restoring the workspace brings all of it back at once. Notifications about that work are the one exception: they are deleted when the workspace is trashed and a restore brings none of them back. See decision:workspace-trash-cascades.

A missing or invalid token gets 401; a signed-in caller who may not do this gets 403, or 404 where a refusal would reveal something hidden from them. An API key acts as its user and needs write scope here; a read-only key gets 403. Rate limit: the /api/tracker/ routes and /api/health together allow 300 requests per 60 seconds per client address (collection endpoints are counted separately); past that the answer is 429 with no retry header, so wait out the window. Superusers are not limited. Every error body is {"status": <code>, "message": "<reason>", "data": {}}; a validation error lists the offending fields under data.
